source.title: The Evolution of Statistical Induction Heads: In-Context Learning Markov Chains
source.authors: Benjamin L. Edelman; Ezra Edelman; Surbhi Goel; Eran Malach; Nikolaos Tsilivis

record.tranche_reason: The study's own results refine a single-transition account: it reports successive incomplete solutions (uniform, unigram, then bigram) and multiple rapid changes, with four stages in the trigram task.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior induction-head findings, but those cited results are not rows. It studies a controlled synthetic Markov-chain task rather than large language models or few-shot task learning. It does not report a bump in the training-loss curve.
record.test_reason: The study trains small attention-only transformers from scratch in a new synthetic setting, in-context Markov chains. It reports its own results on the induction-head mechanism, on abrupt formation, on data dependence, and on multi-stage learning. It does not argue that a version is wrong, so T3 fits better than T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also stress that the switch to bigrams is driven by alignment between layers: the first layer's learning signal depends on the second layer approaching its solution. They frame the unigram stage as a simplicity-bias distractor that delays the induction head. They leave extension to natural-language training as open.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses transformers trained from scratch on synthetic Markov-chain sequences and measures strategy alignment, attention patterns, and test loss; it is not a reproduction of the original natural-language induction-head training setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The speed and staging of learning change with the transition-matrix data distribution and the usefulness of unigram statistics. The reported transition timing also varies across random seeds, while the qualitative dynamics remain consistent.

fits_no_version.finding: In both the minimal model and transformers, the first-layer positional weights develop a spurious even/odd look-back pattern shortly before the induction head forms.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: On the way to the previous-token solution, first-layer positional embeddings transiently favour odd look-back offsets.

record.problems: The evidence concerns small, synthetic tasks and a limited architecture family. The paper describes qualitative curve behaviour without reporting numerical uncertainty for the main comparisons; the 10-seed figure notes variation in transition position but gives no uncertainty interval. It does not test the training-loss bump or large natural-language transformers.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result rows omitted. The theoretical gradient derivations are discussed in the text but are not treated as measurements of the claimed model behaviour.

untested.parts: Bump in the training-loss curve; formation 'early' in training (here it follows a long plateau); natural-language models.
Entire version: no large transformers and no token-index ICL measure.
Entire version: one small architecture family only. The 8-symbol and 2-symbol variants are not cross-family tests.
Entire version: no few-shot task learning studied.
Causal ablation of the heads; natural-language data.

missing.what: Seed variation: 10 seeds show consistent dynamics, but the position of the phase transition varies.
8-symbol transformer shows the same uniform→unigram→bigram stages, but only with sequence length 200.
Single-head models on trigrams cannot beat the bigram strategy; three heads are needed.
Test loss on iid-token and doubly-stochastic distributions over training, for both transformer and minimal model.
Two-symbol transformer vs minimal-model KL-strategy curves, with the alternating positional pattern at 64k examples.
Evidence that layer 2 is learned before layer 1 (sub-steps of formation). Clear in the minimal model and theory; the authors call the transformer evidence 'not so clear'.

record.verdict_notes: R7/R8 were relinked from 'none' to V1, and the fits_no_version entry for them was replaced. The 'NeurIPS 2024' peer-review status is not stated in the supplied text (arXiv v1). No numerical uncertainty is reported, and all main results are read qualitatively from figures.

versions.untested_parts: The mechanism is inspected in the paper's small synthetic setting; it does not establish the claim for other model families or natural-language training.
The paper reports test-loss changes and strategy alignment, not a bump in the training-loss curve. The studied task is synthetic.
The study does not test large transformers or whether induction heads account for most in-context learning in them.
It does not establish induction-head behaviour across model families, model sizes, training runs, other architectures, or modalities.
The data-dependence evidence concerns the synthetic Markov-chain task and altered transition-matrix distributions; other training setups and persistence in natural-language models are not tested.
The paper distinguishes its pattern-copying task from few-shot learning but does not test mechanisms for few-shot task learning.
The multi-stage evidence comes from the synthetic bigram and trigram tasks, not from natural-language model training.

rows.subject: two-layer attention-only transformer
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch; end of training
rows.operation_detail: Inspected attention patterns on a fixed input during training.
rows.baseline: At the start, attention is described as uniform.
rows.value: At the end, the first layer attends to the previous token; the second layer attends to tokens that followed the current token, enabling bigram statistics.
rows.note: The authors describe the final attention pattern as matching their induction-head construction.
rows.check: The link is correct. The heads are 'statistical' induction heads that average over all prior matches, not copy the last one. Evidence is attention on one fixed input (Fig. 2, Fig. 10), with no ablation.

source_check.locator_found: Figure 2; Section 3.1, mechanistic evidence; Appendix B.

rows.subject: two-layer attention-only transformer
rows.operation_detail: Trained on next-token prediction for sequences sampled from Markov chains.
rows.measure: Test loss, measured as KL divergence from the underlying truth
rows.baseline: Unigram and bigram strategy losses are shown as reference lines.
rows.value: The paper describes an initial rapid loss drop, a long period of slight improvement around the unigram strategy, and a second rapid drop toward the Bayes-optimal loss.
rows.note: The paper describes rapid drops in test loss; it does not report a bump in training loss.
rows.check: Test loss (KL), not training loss, so the bump part of V2 is untested. The induction-head drop comes after a long unigram plateau, not early in training. For V7, the stages are preceding incomplete solutions; the paper calls the move to bigrams a single 'rapid phase transition'.

source_check.correct: Partial for V2: the induction-associated second loss drop follows a long unigram plateau. The measured loss is test KL divergence. The strategy sequence supports the tested staging aspect of V7.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1, opening paragraphs; Figure 3 and caption; Section 3.2 discussion accompanying Figure 5.
source_check.problem: An unqualified observed state overstates V2's early-training timing clause.

rows.subject: two-layer attention-only transformer
rows.operation_detail: Compared model predictions with uniform, unigram, and bigram strategies throughout training.
rows.measure: KL divergence between model outputs and the named strategies
rows.value: The model first becomes more similar to the unigram strategy; around the second loss drop, similarity to bigrams increases while similarity to unigrams decreases.
rows.note: The paper identifies the final drop with the transition from the unigram strategy to the bigram strategy.
rows.check: The link is correct. The strategy-alignment curves show the model moving from unigram to bigram around the second drop.

source_check.correct: Partial for V2: strategy alignment confirms an abrupt unigram-to-bigram switch after the prolonged intermediate stage. For V7, this measures strategy stages rather than separately identifying every step of head formation.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1, strategy-alignment paragraph; Figure 3, right panels.
source_check.problem: The alignment result supports the switch but does not establish V2's full early-training pattern.

rows.subject: minimal model (equation 8)
rows.stage_stated: trained with SGD from constant initialization
rows.operation_detail: Trained the simplified model on the ICL-MC task.
rows.measure: Test loss and alignment with uniform, unigram, and bigram strategies
rows.baseline: Uniform, unigram, and bigram strategy references.
rows.value: The model converges to the bigram solution, spending significantly less time, if any, at the unigram solution than the transformer.
rows.note: The paper reports a faster progression than for the transformer.
rows.check: The subject is the minimal linear model of eq. 8, not a transformer. It spends 'significantly less time, if any' at unigrams, so the multi-stage pattern is weak here. Its bearing on V2 is unclear because it is not a transformer, so the V2 link is removed.

source_check.correct: Cannot_determine for V7 from this measurement alone: little or no unigram plateau does not establish that formation lacks separate substeps. Section 3.2 separately analyzes sequential learning of the model's two components.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2, opening paragraph, Lemma 3.1 and Proposition 3.2; Figure 3, bottom.
source_check.problem: The state treats a shortened strategy plateau as evidence of weaker multi-step formation.

rows.subject: two-layer attention-only transformer
rows.operation_detail: Changed the transition-matrix data distribution to vary the usefulness of unigram statistics.
rows.measure: Test loss and speed of convergence
rows.baseline: Training on the original distribution, where unigrams can provide a signal.
rows.value: The no-unigram-signal condition learns faster and avoids a long intermediate plateau, including when evaluated on the original distribution.
rows.note: The paper describes an interpolation among data distributions; the row records the stated comparison at the no-unigram-signal setting.
rows.check: The link is correct. The value is qualitative, read from Fig. 4a's interpolation across distributions, with no numbers given.

rows.subject: three-headed attention-only transformer
rows.measure: Test loss and similarity to unigram, bigram, and trigram strategies
rows.baseline: Uniform, unigram, bigram, and trigram strategies.
rows.value: The model eventually approaches the Bayes-optimal solution; the paper reports four learning stages corresponding to the different strategies, with long plateaus and sudden drops.
rows.note: Single-attention-headed models did not achieve better performance than bigrams; this result is not separately quantified here.
rows.check: No attention or mechanism inspection was done for the trigram model, so the stages are strategy stages, not verified head formation. The layer count is not stated: 'three heads in each layer'.

rows.subject: single-layer transformer
rows.stage_stated: trained for 8 times longer than the two-layer experiments
rows.operation_detail: Trained on ICL-MC and compared with the unigram strategy.

conditions.value: absolute or relative; results reported as applying to both

rows.value: The figure and text report no notable improvement beyond the unigram strategy.
rows.note: This is a depth comparator; the claim versions do not assert that a single-layer transformer should form induction heads.
rows.check: This is not a 'none' row. A single-layer model failing to beat unigrams, even with 8x training, fits V1's requirement of cross-layer composition. The state means the V1-consistent pattern was observed, not that the induction behaviour appeared.

relationships.reason: At the end of training, layer 1 attends to the previous token and layer 2 to tokens following matches (R1). Single-layer models never pass unigrams (R7, R8).
